subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF GILL REPORT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
CONSIDERATION OF GILL REPORT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this stage to ask leave, in accordance with standing order 26, to move the adjournment of the house to discuss an urgent matter of national importance with regard to the report which was submitted almost two years ago by the royal commission on the administration and application of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
We have asked a number of questions on the subject and tried to get some information, but without too much success.
The government is studying the report, but we have not been informed of the results of that study. At present every member must face problems dealing with unemployment insurance and the operation of the unemployment insurance commission in his own riding.
The unemployed are affected and are victimized, that is, half a million persons out of work are affected by the functioning of that agency. Furthermore, the officials find themselves in an impasse, since they must apply the act as it exists, and sometimes it is unjust and very poorly drafted.
The government has been studying this report for several months, but the house was not informed of the results of the study; we do not know the opinion of the government or what it intends to do. If such an inquiry proved to be very useful and necessary two years ago, it is even more so today, especially if we take into account the unemployment situation.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier), the
adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the immediate need on the part of the house to take the immediate action necessary for the duty in committee of the Gill report and to carry out as soon as possible the recommendations of the said committee in order to correct numerous anomalies in the operation of the unemployment insurance commission.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF GILL REPORT-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Are there any other hon. members who wish to say anything on this request to adjourn the house under standing order 26 in order to give more attention to the Gill report? If not I am prepared to render a decision.
Standing order 26, of course, envisages something which is a sudden emergency. Citation 100 (8) of Beauchesne's fourth edition says, in the middle of the paragraph:
What I think was contemplated was an occurrence of some sudden emergency, either in home or in foreign affairs.
I think all hon. members would agree that this matter has been raised several times during the question period. It is not exactly a new matter and to my way of thinking it is not a new, sudden emergency. In my opinion it does not conform to the dictates of standing order 26; therefore I must decide that the proceedings of the house should not be set aside at this time to proceed with the matter set forth in the motion submitted to me.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON INQUIRY AS TO PROVISION FOR STUDY

Yesterday the hon. member for Saint John-Albert inquired about discussions I had held with the premiers of the Atlantic provinces regarding the proposed railway legislation. At the time of those discussions last week I explained that because of the complexities of the problems of transportation in the Atlantic provinces a decision had been taken when the new legislation was first under consideration by the previous administration -and this decision was confirmed by the present administration-that the questions relating to the Maritime Freight Rates Act which had been brought forward by the royal commission on transportation should be the subject of a separate examination. The current railway legislation does not deal with these particular recommendations, although 

it maintains the protection accorded to the Atlantic provinces under the Maritime Freight Rates Act as extended by the government of the day early in 1957.
I am sure hon. members will be glad to hear that the Minister of Transport will be back at his desk within a few days. At that time we intend to give prompt consideration to the establishment of a special examination into the problems relating to maritime transportation and the Maritime Freight Rates Act which were raised by the royal commission.
The provincial representatives at the discussion to which I am referring also raised the question whether the proposed railway legislation would lead to a further deterioration with regard to rate problems in the Atlantic provinces. I indicated that the intent of the legislation was to retain all the existing advantages and statutory protection accorded by the Maritime Freight Rates Act. Given this situation, the new legislation might be expected to be more advantageous on an overall basis than the situation which has applied heretofore, in which rate increases took place on a broad horizontal basis. Nevertheless, the points raised by the provincial premiers in this regard are being further reviewed on our part.

I wonder if subclause 5 is not at variance with subclause 1 of section 17, because I feel the commission could easily give the following interpretation to subclause 5: since there is no evidence likely to be of interest to the commission, the commission will not be required to sit at the place scheduled for that date.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of subclause 4 is to maintain the ten days notice to the commission. Under the bill as originally proposed, with the 15 days and then ten days before the commencement of the sittings, it allowed only five days for the public to become aware of a sitting, after publication of the notice, and to make up their minds after studying the advertisement whether they wished to make representations. Then they had to prepare a synopsis of their representations and get it into the hands of the secretary to the commission. Frankly that was impossible. That is why there has been the insistence on the 30 days notice. Now that the minister has brought forward the 30 days amendment, notice must be given within 20 days after the date of publication. This means that the commission will get ten clear days notice. I think that is basically the same requirement in subclause 4 as it now stands as it is in the proposed amendment. I would have thought that was not necessary. I would have thought it would be adequate to give five days notice.
My notes in the original instance on examination of this bill indicate that five days notice would be sufficient, and therefore we could take the proposed amendment of the minister by saying "within 25 days of the date of hearing". I think the purpose of the notice is to give the public the chance to study the proposals and make their representations. It must be remembered that you will be dealing in many instances with really untrained persons, in so far as making representations before public bodies is concerned. They are not going to go running to high priced counsel to make these representations. Therefore every latitude should be given to the public in this regard.
It may be a little bit of tough luck on the commission, but in any event the subject is somewhat limited. I do not know how many representations will be received, say in the province of Alberta, with regard to 17 seats as the matter now stands. Ontario, regionally might be somewhat greater. But I do feel, and suggest to the minister, that at this time we should bear in mind that publication in the Canada Gazette at the first of the month
[The Chairman.]

will perhaps not get to the people until the third of the month, and if it is a newspaper circulated in a province, by the time it gets to the rural areas three or four days may have been eaten up. Let us give the public the benefit of any latitude that can be given. Therefore instead of saying "20 days from the date of publication", why not say 25 days, giving the commissions five days before the sittings? I think this would be quite adequate. I put my point forward on that basis, Mr. Chairman. There is a proposal for a subclause 5 and I am going to have something to say about that, but I am dealing with subclause 4 at the present time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am advised, and I think there is considerable validity in this view, that the commissions will require more than five days between the moment a representation is received and the time a hearing is held. This is regarded as the irreducible minimum in order to give the commissions an opportunity to sift out the representations. There may be many representations received by a commission and it may not be possible for them to get ready for a hearing and hold it in five days. We think ten days is the minimum they ought to have. I put that forward as a reason why the provision which is contained in the amended subclause 4 ought to be maintained.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION

Mr. Chairman, the minister will readily understand that in certain areas of the country time will be taken up by what might be called the portal to portal requirements in connection with notice reaching interested people. Then they have to prepare their representations and get them into the hands of the secretary. Anywhere from seven to ten days may elapse as a result. Therefore what I am concerned about is the time allotted to the public to study the proposals, make up their minds and then prepare their representations. I am concerned that this time is being squeezed. After all, there will be a deadline imposed by the secretary to the commission, and if they say representations will be received until five o'clock on a certain day, and that is ten days before the sittings, difficulties might arise for the public. In this regard I would ask the minister, just how complicated can these representations be? The commissioners may have to bend over a little more, I will admit; but my concern is primarily for the public, unless the intention is to insist that they go to high priced counsel to prepare these briefs and get them in. I think we would be erring on

the side of restriction rather than on being generous with the public.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I just want to say a few words in support of the views expressed by the hon. member for Edmonton West with respect to increasing the number of days to 25. Let us consider the situation. The commissions will be well versed in the electoral boundaries of the ridings with which they are concerned, because they will have studied them and set those boundaries. They will know the conditions that exist in the constituencies with which they are concerned. On the other hand, when a notice appears to the general public it will not be the individual who will be making the representation as much as groups of people interested in the political affairs of that particular constituency. No one person in that organization is going to make the necessary decision as to whether or not representations should be made. Meetings will have to be called; they will have to prepare themselves and look at the situation, all of which will take a longer time than it would take the commission to acquaint themselves with the representations they have already carefully studied in the setting out of the electoral boundaries. Therefore I think if we are to decide which way it should go the benefit should be given to those people who are not acquainted with what is going on but who are anxious, after careful consideration resulting from a number of meetings, to decide whether or not they should make a representation, and also to decide what form the representation should take.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to support the argument which has been raised for a greater length of time, and I should like to quote an example to the minister from northern Ontario, where I imagine at the first redistribution there will be the most difficulty. You will have a situation where there would be five ridings to which probably some adjustments will be made. They cover a distance of roughly 700 miles from east to west and 600 miles from north to south, with communities scattered all along the way. I would point here to Kenora-Rainy River, where some communities involving several thousand voters could be on the margins of boundaries with as much as 300 or 400 miles between them.
Another point is that there is no single newspaper which reaches this region. There is no radio station or television station in this region. The watersheds of influence and information are tremendously varied and the changes which will be necessary as a result of any commission hearings and subsequent redistribution will be substantial. If I may give one example, it is quite possible that the constituency of Port Arthur, which is going to be cut considerably, is likely to have some relationship with Kapuskasing and

even Timmins; yet there is no normal centre for any communication between these two places at all. For that reason I think the time mentioned is really minimal; it is very narrow.
I think the minister is aware that during elections there is an extra time allowance for certain of the northern ridings because of their area, and it is a rather substantial time allowance in relationship to the total electoral period. It seems to me that very same argument applies in this case. Therefore I should like to support the arguments which have been put forward by the hon. member for Edmonton West regarding the time factor. I like the improvement to this clause suggested by the minister but I think he can be even more generous.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the minister has been very kind in accepting certain suggestions, but perhaps the way out of this dilemma would be to leave the ten day period and make the notice 40 days. However, the controversial changes are going to be those where townships and towns are changed. Perhaps the minister would accept the 40 days notice and the ten day period, because in fairness to everyone five days is a short period of time for the commission to prepare for representations.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am rather surprised that the minister has come forward with this proposed amendment, because it represents a judgment without a hearing. 1 could not for a moment accept it. It may be that in a case where there are no representations the commission would not be required to sit, although it has given notice of a hearing, but we could not possibly accept this amendment in its present form. It states "the nature of the representation as indicated in the notice is such that no such hearing is necessary." We are giving carte blanche to the commission to reject, in theory, any representation, yet the machinery of the act does not provide for any appeal from the commission's decision in this regard. Again I think public interest demands that any representations made must be heard. After all, the requirement is only on the basis of a concise representation as referred to in subclause 4. Therefore, representations could be dismissed out of hand on the basis of a precis or synthesis of a representation to be made, and there is no appeal whatsoever from a commission's decision.

Electoral Boundaries Commissions notice is such that no such hearing is necessary".
We are changing the boundaries of the ridings only every 10 years and it is a very final thing. The President of the Privy Council has suggested that one case might be where the commission is prepared to accept the suggestion of a group. This happens every day with the Ontario municipal board. bilingual advertising in Quebec city and not in Prince Edward Island where, according to official data, 8.8 per cent of the people are French speaking?
I respectfully submit, therefore, that all publicity from the federal government should be bilingual, no matter what part of the country it is meant for. If within a period of 30 days from the day the copy of the report of any commission for a province is laid before the House of Commons or published pursuant to section 19-

Let us try to analyse the situation, human nature being what it is. Let us consider, for example, commission A. That commission hears representations and draws a map. All of the possible objections will have been raised at its hearings. If parliament simply goes through a perfunctory operation, and not one based at all on consideration, because one quarter of the members from the province in question, over which commission A has authority object, the matter goes back to the commission. Anyone who has ever reargued a case in a court which has originally come to a conclusion, yet for some reason a reargument is considered necessary, knows what the difficulties are. The difficulties in a court under those circumstances would be much less than the difficulties of bringing these objections again before the same commission that had decided earlier, on the basis of what it had heard and the evidence placed before it, as to the course to be followed. The commission would simply meet and say, "Under the law 25 per cent of the members from the province have objected. We dealt with this matter and it has come back to us purely as a mechanical result of the statute as it exists, but that is the end of it".
I have a great deal of regard for public opinion, and if a wrong is done, or a mistake is made, and 25 per cent of the members from any one province object, then in a debate the searchlight of scrutiny and examination will be brought to bear on what has taken place, and where there has been unfairness public opinion often steps in. If it does not step in at the time, it steps in later on whenever there is an opportunity for the people to vote.
I am not going into particulars in this regard, but I know something about this because I had an experience which was spoken of at the time. I do not think any member of this house ever went through two gerrymanderings, but I did go through two of them. This is what we are trying to get away from. As a matter of fact, as I said to the minister in the course of a private conversation recently, if it had not been for the gerrymander of 1949 I would never have sought re-election to parliament. However, that operation took place without anaesthetic and the results were most favourable to me in the long run.

That was public opinion operating in consequence of what was believed to be an injustice. This has happened to members in all parts of the house. None of us has been guiltless in connection with arranging constituencies of political opponents in such a way that their hopes of return were considerably diminished, and that has been so throughout the years.
We are now doing away with that sort of thing, but in doing away with it we must preserve the authority of parliament. Parliament must have the final say and the opportunity to speak. We cannot, as parliamentarians, abdicate the rights of parliament to a commission. Otherwise the first responsibility of parliament, the assurance of fair representation, is completely denied-whether in fact or in theory, none the less actually, under statute.
Members of this house as a whole, I am sure, would agree that we dare not pass an amendment which simply provides for a perfunctory return to the commission of an objection, because it has been raised by one quarter of the members of a province, without debate in this chamber. To do otherwise would be to make the commission in effect the absolute authority.

Act. At the present time we have 263 seats in the House of Commons, allocated among the provinces, and one seat each for the Yukon and Northwest Territories. Section 52 of the British North America Act states that this number is not sacred. What is sacred are the rules which regulate the number of seats to which each of the provinces is entitled after each decennial census.
I could read the rules which are contained in section 51 of the British North America Act, but what they mean is, once a new decennial census has been made, and the resulting figures have been published and a readjustment effected, one must apply the rules contained in section 51 in respect of proportionment. We have been very careful in this regard not to apply the limitation to numbers of proportionate representatives in the House of Commons as prescribed by the constitution of Canada. Until there is a change in section 51 of the British North America Act by amendment, as the result of the consent of the parliament of Canada and seven provinces representing 50 per cent of the population, the principles spelled out in section 51, in so far as the proportions to which each province is respectively entitled in the House of Commons, will have

Mr. Chairman, in spite of the explanations made by the Minister of Justice, some ambiguities remain in so far as this subclause is concerned.
As I understand the situation, under section 51 of the British North America Act there are certain rules in respect of the decision as to how many members there shall be, and how they shall be distributed among the provinces, taking into consideration such things as the senatorial floor. However, under the proposed amendment to section 51 of the British North America Act I envisage this problem. The minister suggests that whenever the proportionate number of representatives for the provinces is to be changed, such change requires the consent of seven of the ten provinces representing 50 per cent or more of the population. Presumably we must decide this proportion by calculating the total population of Canada and dividing that population by, as at the present time, 263 members. But if there is a shift in the population which, using this mathematical calculation, would in fact change the number of seats that would be assigned to the provinces, then according to what the Minister of Justice is now telling us it would seem that in spite of the change indicated by the mathematical calculation it will require agreement by seven out of the ten provinces representing more than 50 per cent of the people of Canada before the number of seats in a province can be changed.
I understood the minister to say this would be the effect of the proposed method of amending section 51 of the British North America Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION

No, Mr. Chairman. I agree that the words I used might have been a little too technical, and when I say that I hope the hon. gentleman will not take offence because whenever one deals with the words of one's own profession he sometimes makes the mistake of using them to too great an extent.
I did not say that if there was a change in the relative population of all the prov-

inces as shown by a new decennial census you would need the consent of seven provinces to increase the number of representatives of one province whose population has increased very much, and to decrease the representation of another province whose population has decreased. What I said, and the hon. member has referred to it, is that it is completely ruled or regulated by the principles of section 51 of the British North America Act which establishes the relationship between the population of a province in relation to the over-all population of Canada and the number of seats which that population will entitle the province to in relation to the over-all number of seats in the House of Commons. So if the amending formula is adopted its precise effect will be that this rule, this proportion or this relativity will continue in effect. Each 10 years we will have to determine, in accordance with the new census and according to the rules which exist at present, in what proportion and to what extent the relative number of seats to which each province is entitled will change.
What I said was that to change the rules in accordance with which we do that every 10 years, to change the proportionality, if I may express myself that way, we will need to amend the constitution of Canada. We will need to change section 51 of the British North America Act and enact a new proportion. In other words, we know at present that if the province of Ontario has a population of 6,500,000, let us say, it is entitled to so many seats in the over-all total of 265. If 10 years from now the new census shows that the population of Ontario is then nine million people and Quebec is down to three million, in applying the rule at present found in section 51 of the constitution the relationship or proportion will be maintained but there will be a new number of seats to which Ontario will be entitled and a fewer number of seats to which Quebec will be entitled. That proportion under the formula, not the number of seats but the rule of proportionality-that is why we use that word in subsection (g) of section 6-will be maintained. Does that answer the question?

Act. Therefore there is no question in this bill of changing the rule of proportionality.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like an explanation from the sponsor of the bill. Electoral Boundaries Commissions

But if a draft representation order has precisely been accepted by the House of Commons and the Senate, in a word, by all, and approved by the governor in council for certain provinces only, and not for everyone of them, will the effective date start immediately for the provinces whose draft representation order has been accepted and not for the others?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: But that does not prevent the house being furnished with copies of the reports, under clauses 18 and 19, seriatim as they come in.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: In other words, we may get little dribs and drabs in that regard.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
I have a point to raise in connection with this clause. If you do not mind, Mr. Chairman, I will read the clause.
Within five days after the receipt by the Secretary of State of the draft representation order, the governor in council shall by proclamation declare the draft representation order to be in force, effective upon the dissolution of the then existing parliament-
Then the second part of the clause reads as follows:
-or effective upon the dissolution of the next following parliament if upon the issue of the proclamation parliament is then dissolved, and upon the issue of the proclamation the order shall have the force of law accordingly.
I want to draw the attention of the committee to the first part of that clause where it indicates an order being effective upon the dissolution of the then existing parliament. Under our parliamentary system in Canada and under parliamentary systems elsewhere there have been occasions when governments have somewhat unexpectedly been retired from office. It might well happen that a parliament expecting to continue for two, three, or four more years might proceed to proclaim an order to be effective upon the dissolution of the then existing parliament, believing that dissolution would not occur for a year or two years. Suddenly a crisis might develop and parliament might be dissolved within a week or even a shorter period. We would then be faced with a most difficult situation in the organization of constituencies whose boundaries had been substantially altered.
I confess I have not pursued this thought to any finality; I have not pursued it to the point at which I am prepared to suggest some amendment to provide authority under which the effect of what I am now suggesting could happen would be deferred. The second part of the clause is, I think, all right, although I judge it might be unusual for the proclamation to be issued after parliament had been dissolved. But I wonder whether the minister has given any consideration to the point I have raised. If it is not a valid point I am prepared to have my error disclosed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
I think the point made by the hon. gentleman is, in one way, a technical one because it would be impossible for the chief electoral officer to conduct an election on such short notice without having the forms printed for the new ridings and the

Electoral Boundaries Commissions machinery of the election organized. It would not be possible for him to complete these arrangements within the 60 days provided under the Canada Elections Act. I do not think it would be possible for any government to contemplate such an action.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Suppose it is beaten.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: That is the point my hon. friend made. There is a sudden cessation of life of the government. In other words, it is defeated.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Would not the chief electoral officer simply have to make the decision? The hon. member is taking the position that proclamation would already have been made-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Oh yes. The representation order has been presented and the law is mandatory in this regard. It says five days. There is no one who can control it. This is an area in which one must tread very carefully.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: May I present the problem differently? Suppose a government did not wish to have an election under the new electoral boundary arrangements. Suppose it knew a proclamation was to be issued. It could bring about in various ways the dissolution of parliament and then it could have an election under the old boundary arrangements because the new boundaries would not become effective until there was a new parliament. Thus it is not obligatory on a government, once this machinery gets going, to have an election on the basis of the new boundaries which are to be put forward.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: I think the hon. member is making a valid point. This could happen, but there is an inexorable movement of time envisaged by this bill. Any government would have to take this movement of time into account. In other words, if it intended to do as the hon. member suggested, dissolution would have to take place-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Before the fatal ten days.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
That is right. I do not know how it could be avoided. I agree that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has raised an important point. I am advised that this matter has been considered and wrestled with but that nobody has been able to provide a solution which would meet this problem of the proclamation of the draft order occurring, let us say, two weeks before a dissolution. There would obviously be a great problem in the constituencies. I would certainly be glad to hear any views from the


committee as to how to meet this situation, or how it could be avoided. I would point out that the government itself would be faced with the same chaotic problem with respect to its own electoral ridings and would not likely resort to the procedure suggested, and would seek to time a dissolution so as to avoid the difficulty to which the hon. member referred. However, as the hon. member for Edmonton West pointed out, when a government is defeated dissolution is inevitable. In that eventuality, of course, the timing would be known to the other parties in the house.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: A thought which occurs to me is this: The decennial census is taken up in years the dates of which are fixed. On the other hand, terms of parliament are irregular. A situation could arise where a new redistribution had just been completed at a time when a parliament was almost at the end of its life. What would happen in these circumstances? It would be obligatory to dissolve parliament. Would the proclamation necessary under this legislation be delayed so that the new parliament could be elected under the old redistribution arrangements, despite the fact that a census had recently been taken?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: There is theoretical validity about the point which the hon. member raises-

speechtext: I have not figured it out, but I know there is a census taken every ten years and the average life of a parliament used to be four years. One period does not divide into the other evenly. The situation to which I have referred might occur every few years.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: It would happen, no doubt, but in the case cited a government would be required to run its full term of five years before it would be involved in the kind of situation the hon. member has outlined. This is not a frequent occurrence; in fact, it is very rare.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, with regard to clause 25 (2) I just want to underline to the minister one of the dangers with regard to the names of territorial divisions. Electoral Boundaries Commissions ister could elucidate on the point I have raised.

speechtext: In this regard, Mr. Chairman, I have the suspicion that there will be some unforeseen results from the passage of this clause, in that at the time of proclaiming a representation order the appointments of all returning officers holding offices shall terminate, and there shall then be a renomination of all returning officers. If that is the situation I think this committee should be made aware of it. Is that what is contemplated by the government under this clause? If there is going to be a complete refashioning of constituencies, and section 29 of the Representation Act is being repealed, and the ridings in respect of which these returning officers hold positions disappear, their appointments will disappear. Is that contemplated by this clause?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps I may be allowed to comment in respect of that point. This matter was raised before the committee on privileges and elections during its consideration and review of the Canada Elections Act. That act provides, as I recall it, that as soon as the boundaries of a riding are changed in any way, or the riding itself is changed in any way, the returning officer's office is vacant, and the riding is considered 

as a new riding. I understand that to be the situation under the existing act.
One of the matters that was considered by that committee was whether these offices should be made permanent. I think the hon. member will recall that under the Canada Elections Act, as passed in 1960, these positions became vacant. That is one of the provisions of the Canada Elections Act which I do not think should necessarily be covered by this bill. Perhaps a discussion of this particular point should properly take place during a consideration or revision of the Canada Elections Act.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on that point I believe that the subject is important enough. Indeed, in the constituencies the returning officers are appointed by the government in office, and often these appointments are-I do not speak for my constituency, far from it- but in several constituencies these are political appointments and the returning officer is there to protect the interest of the party in office. Therefore, I feel that this is a major point to decide.
In the event that new boundaries are fixed, will all the returning officers presently appointed lose their jobs and will others be appointed by the government?
If that is the case, we should provide, before going through with this, a new procedure for appointing returning officers in the constituencies, because in many cases the actions of some returning officers give rise to complaints. Thus, we fear that with another party in office, or a change of government, returning officers would also change and we would constantly be faced with the same problems, for any time there would be a change of government there would also be a change of returning officers, or a way would be found to amend the act in order to be able to appoint new returning officers.
Therefore, I think a new procedure should be devised for the appointment of returning officers, in order that appointments be made in a manner which would be fair and equitable to all candidates in an election.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Let us consider clause 27. As I understand the situation, a representation order does not come into effect until a dissolution of parliament. This clause permits a representation order to take the effect of law whenever it is proclaimed, so that returning officers can be appointed under the Canada Elections Act for ridings that are

designated in the representation order. In other words, by bringing it into effect in respect of the returning officers, it is possible to appoint the returning officers before a dissolution.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR BOUNDARIES COMMISSIONS AND READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: May I ask how you would have them vacate their offices?

If the representation order establishes a particular constituency with a new name, for example, and if there is a returning officer for Inverness-Richmond or Digby-Annapolis-Kings and the new riding is-

speechtext: But the act does not come into force until dissolution and therefore the newly designated constituency does not come into force until dissolution and the old riding does not disappear until dissolution. Reasons for vacating his office, such as the returning officer no longer living in the constituency, do not apply because the constituency does not come into being until dissolution. So what are we going to be faced with? A vast number of returning officers being out of office on the dissolution of parliament and then a whole new group taking over on the first day of the election period.

maintopic: TRADE-VISIT TO CANADA OF U.K. HOME BUILDERS MISSION
TRADE-VISIT TO CANADA OF U.K. HOME BUILDERS MISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the voice of the Kootenays I addressed a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce on orders of the day today with respect to the visit to Canada of the home builders mission from Britain to study the Canadian timber trade, housing methods and so on and asked him if arrangements could be made for this very important mission to visit the Kootenays while en route from Vancouver to Calgary.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this is an important mission as indicated by the news release issued by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, which reads as follows:
A 26 member home builders mission from Britain will arrive in Vancouver on October 15 for a two week tour of this country to study Canadian timber frame housing construction methods. Sponsored by the Department of Trade and Commerce, the mission will comprise ten directors of British housing construction firms, and representatives of the British government's ministry of public building and works, the royal institute of British architects, the national building agency, the London county council, the timber trade federation of the United Kingdom the British woodwork manufacturers association and British building societies and trade unions. The mission will visit Vancouver, Calgary, Toronto and Ottawa.
The release goes on to describe the purpose of the mission, which is a most interesting one.
One of the primary purposes of the home builders mission will be to study Canada's timber frame construction methods and their application to a wide variety of dwelling designs. Members will also have an opportunity to see the milling of Canadian surfaced lumber and the manufacture of softwood and hardwood plywoods. Canadian builders and lumber interests will also have an opportunity to meet the British builders to discuss possible ways of participating in Britain's accelerated housing program.
This is a mission which is of great importance to all Canadians, of importance to the Canadian economy, and of particular importance to the forest products producing areas; and I happen to represent one of the largest and most important forest products producing areas in Canada.
The reasons for my suggesting this visit are several. First of all, the Kootenays have often been overlooked when arrangements were being made by this and former governments for groups in other countries visiting

Canada. If I had time I could give several illustrations of this, but I shall only mention one, which was when the British forestry commission visited Canada. It visited certain areas interested in forest production and certain other areas, but it overlooked one of the highest producing yield areas in Canada, the Kootenays. This has been noted by the industry and by the organizations in the constituency which I have the honour to represent.
I also make this suggestion because the Kootenay forest production area people are interested in the expansion of markets, both domestic and foreign, including markets in Great Britain. Third, we have a particular type of species in the Kootenays and interior B.C., a very high quality species, and high quality producing species, which is treated in the processing plants there. Fourth, we have a varied type of house construction, and the uses of timber for housing and other purposes in that area would be very interesting for these visitors to see. Fifth, if they visited this area they would have the opportunity to meet the local people, the local operators, and discuss questions which would be of mutual concern to them both.
It would also provide an opportunity for these visitors to witness different methods of production, and compare those methods with the ones used in other parts of Canada. We have, in the Kootenays, some of the most up to date mills and producing plants in Canada. Finally, such a visit would give them an opportunity to enjoy most unusual scenery and unparalleled natural beauty.
I urge that even at this late date consideration be given to having this mission visit the Kootenays and the interior of B.C. while en route from Vancouver to Calgary. Further-
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion more I urge upon ministers in this government that in future, when arrangements are being made for these visiting groups, whether they represent agriculture, labour, the forest industry, the mining industry or any other industry, to consider the interior of B.C. and the Kootenay area in particular, areas which have been often overlooked during previous visits. I should like the parliamentary secretary to let me know whether arrangements can be made, or whether he can promise that in the future the situation will be remedied.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Luc Pepin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: TRADE-VISIT TO CANADA OF U.K. HOME BUILDERS MISSION
speechtext:
May I say I am quite sure the minister will read with great interest the wise remarks made by the hon. member.
In the meantime I wish to make it clear that the mission has come to Canada, not so much to look at our forests or to enjoy the landscape, even the landscape of the beautiful Kootenays, as to inspect Canadian building methods and techniques of timber frame construction. This is part of a program designed to demonstrate the advantages of timber frame construction using Canadian lumber and plywood, and allied building materials.
The mission which is now in Vancouver already has a very heavy program of visiting construction sites, building associations and government agencies across the country. Therefore it would be difficult, if not impossible, to fit a visit to the Kootenays into its program. However, approximately 30 per cent of the total time of the mission in Canada will be spent in British Columbia and this should be a source of satisfaction to the hon. member.
